name: Sara Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to companies, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Sara Okafor, 58, and I joined the line crew late after getting my vocational certificate. I load cones and tools before dawn, help isolate a circuit, then work under a senior lineworker’s eye while we repair overhead lines for the electricity company. I like seeing the lights return on a street. I’m still slow at some fittings, and the lower junior pay leaves little room once rent and my partner’s medicine are paid.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you in this work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wanted a trade I could do with my hands, and I’m proud when my crew trusts me with more. My grown children have their own homes, so I’m not paying school bills now. My partner Eli fixes bicycles when his joints allow, but we cannot count on that money. I use an AI app most evenings to review safety terms, then check every answer against the printed manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the poles still need people, and a computer clearing paperwork is fine by me. Our foreman can keep his fancy forecasts if the crew still gets a safe truck and enough time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I’d still be counting days until payday. The company could trim junior shifts for reasons that have nothing to do with AI, and there are few line crews around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep taking the early truck and asking Mara, our senior lineworker, to check my terminations. Starting now I’d put forty from each pay into an emergency envelope; in 2029, the first full year after this picture settles, I’d keep doing that and use the app for safety revision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady on the actual line, but not steady at the kitchen table. One missed week would nearly empty what we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does less than a month saved mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less than one month of bills, even with the envelope started. Eli’s medicine comes before anything pleasant, so the first cut would be our weekly café lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your confidence in the trade stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I trust the craft more than the roster. My certificate did not promise a full set of shifts, and I’m the junior person when work is scarce.

say: I’d tell the crew **line repair** still needs hands and safe equipment.
I’d welcome **lighter paperwork** if it does not squeeze repair time.
think: I’m worried **junior shifts** could disappear despite little AI change.
My household has **under a month** of bills saved and few nearby line jobs.
do: Keep taking the **early truck** and ask Mara to check terminations.
Put **forty per pay** into an emergency envelope and review safety terms.
feel: I feel **steady at work** but uneasy about one missed week of pay.
S0.quote: I trust the craft more than the roster.
fieldNote: Sara takes visible pride in each **safe repair**, despite being a junior hire at 58.
Her claim that poles need people sits beside a much sharper worry about **unreliable shifts** and almost no cash buffer.

steps.text: Take the early line truck and continue supervised repairs
Put forty from each pay into an emergency envelope
Review safety terms in the AI app against the printed manual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that software might sort orders and outage reports, while our hands still make the line safe. I would also say we should learn the new dispatch screen instead of pretending it will vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the first squeeze is the number of truck crews sent out, not a robot on a pole. If planning gets cheaper, management may pack more calls into one shift and leave the junior worker home on quiet days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the foreman for a supervised turn entering closeout notes on the new tablet, and I’d practice with the AI app after dinner. In 2029 I’d keep repair shifts if offered, but I’d apply to the local depot for a stores role if our crew hours fell twice in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be interested in the screen and nervous about the roster at the same time. I can learn quickly, but I cannot pay rent with curiosity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you apply for if shifts fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the fuses and clamps by touch after loading the truck, though I would need training on stock records. The depot is the one other employer I can reach without moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you work with a sceptical colleague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would offer to enter our notes while Mara checks them, because she knows what a wrong record can do. I would not ask her to trust a suggestion without testing it on the line.

say: I’d tell coworkers **dispatch software** can ease reports while crews still make repairs safe.
I’d ask the crew to **learn the screen** and test its suggestions.
think: I fear faster planning will **reduce crew hours**, especially mine as a junior.
My rent depends on shifts, and the **nearby depot** is my only clear fallback.
do: Request a **supervised tablet turn** recording completed line repairs.
Apply for a **depot stores role** if crew hours fall twice in a month.
feel: I feel **curious** about new tools and nervous about rent.
S1.quote: I can learn quickly, but I cannot pay rent with curiosity.
fieldNote: Her interest in new tools is specific: she wants to **enter closeout notes** under supervision.
The fallback is narrow and concrete, because only one **reachable depot** offers a plausible opening near her home.

steps.text: Practice closeout notes on the crew tablet and AI app
Apply for a depot stores role after two short crew months
Keep taking line repair shifts while offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI by 2028 could run the schedules, but the crew must still test for voltage with their own instruments. I would ask the company what happens to people on the pole when capable robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the thinking system arrives and 63 when robots reach the physical work. That gap might buy me shifts, but a junior worker with thin savings cannot bank on being kept until retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I’d ask the training lead to let me shadow cable testing, which uses judgment and equipment I barely know. In 2029 I’d take every safe paid shift, apply for a depot stores opening if one appeared, and cut the café lunches; when robots reached line repairs around 2031 I’d ask for placement before my crew was cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m frightened by how fast the calendar moves. I could still show up smiling at the morning briefing, then lie awake over the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra cable skill remain useful after robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I cannot claim it would. The point is to earn a wider place on the payroll while there is still a human crew; I would need paid instruction rather than another bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if shifts stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Eli that his bicycle money cannot carry our rent if my line shifts end. We would list medicine and rent first, then speak to our grown children about temporary help only if we had to.

say: I’d tell the crew **thinking AI** may schedule us by 2028, while line repairs stay hands-on until around 2031.
I’d ask the company for a **robot transition** plan before crews shrink.
think: I’m 60 at AGI and **63 at robots**, with too little cash to assume retirement.
I expect junior **line shifts** could disappear when robots can work safely.
do: Shadow **cable testing** now if paid instruction is available.
Take paid shifts in 2029 and **apply to depot stores** if an opening appears.
Cut **café lunches** and request placement before robot crews displace us.
feel: I feel **frightened** by a short runway and uncertain rent.
S2.quote: I could still show up smiling at the morning briefing, then lie awake over the rent.
fieldNote: She separates the 2028 **thinking change** from the 2031 threat to physical repair shifts.
Cable testing is an effort to stay employed temporarily, and Sara explicitly rejects any claim that the skill makes her **robot proof**.

steps.text: Shadow cable testing with paid instruction from the training lead
Take every safe paid line shift in 2029
Apply for a depot stores opening when advertised
Stop weekly café lunches to protect rent and medicine money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers that five years is enough to ask clear questions, but not enough to promise everyone another trade. The system could take our planning in 2031; the physical repair work faces robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 I might still need wages, and at 66 the robot change could reach me before I can afford to stop. The extra years would let me build savings, but only if our shifts stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep putting forty per pay aside and ask for paid cable-testing instruction this winter. During 2032, after the thinking system arrives, I’d volunteer for the inspection roster if it still used people; before 2034 I’d apply to depot stores rather than wait for my own crew to close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered than in the fast picture. There is still a long, uncomfortable stretch between a plan on paper and rent actually paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you try to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months of rent and medicine would let us breathe; at forty per pay it will take years. I would raise the amount only if I get more shifts, not promise money we do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does inspection last once robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not call it safe once robots can climb and inspect. I want a chance to keep earning while the company sorts its crews, then I need an actual placement or opening.

say: I’d ask for **clear company answers** during the five years before AGI.
I’d distinguish 2031 **planning changes** from hands-on robot work around 2034.
think: I may need wages at **66**, when capable robots arrive.
My savings plan depends on **steady shifts** that the company has not promised.
do: Set aside **forty per pay** and request paid cable-testing instruction.
Volunteer for a **human inspection roster** in 2032 if one remains.
Apply to **depot stores** before robots reach repairs in 2034.
feel: I feel **less cornered**, though the rent still makes the long plan fragile.
S3.quote: There is still a long, uncomfortable stretch between a plan on paper and rent actually paid.
fieldNote: The longer warning lets her name a **three-month savings goal**, while she recognizes forty per pay will take years.
She treats inspection as continued paid work during transition, then seeks an actual **depot opening** before robots can perform it.

steps.text: Put forty from each pay toward three months of rent and medicine
Request paid cable-testing instruction this winter
Volunteer for a paid human inspection roster in 2032
Apply to depot stores before robot line crews arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my friends that a decade gives workers time to make choices, if the company tells the truth about its plans. By 2036 thinking AI could handle the records, and around 2039 robots could do the line repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the first date and 71 at the robot date. I hope to be retired by then, but with less than a month saved today I cannot call it a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the line job now, raise my envelope deposit from forty to sixty only when overtime pays, and ask the company about its retirement terms in writing. In 2037 I’d take a paid inspection shift if my body and the roster allow; before 2039 I’d decide with Eli whether we can stop working or need the depot position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe with ten years on the clock. I still dislike planning old age around shifts I might never get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What facts would settle the retirement decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The actual pension statement, if there is a pension, plus our rent and medicine costs. I have not checked the terms, so I would not tell Eli we are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your body changes before the technology does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply to depot stores while I can still lift boxes, and ask for shorter assignments if the company offers them. I will not climb just to prove I am tough when my knees say otherwise.

say: I’d say a **decade of warning** could let lineworkers choose, if company plans are honest.
I’d explain 2036 **record changes** come before hands-on robots around 2039.
think: I hope to retire before **71**, but current savings cannot guarantee it.
My own **pension terms** are unknown until I request a statement.
do: Keep **line shifts** now and put extra overtime money aside.
Request a **written retirement statement** before making a stopping date.
Take paid inspection work in **2037** if health and roster permit.
feel: I feel **able to breathe**, though uncertain wages make old age difficult to plan.
S4.quote: I hope to be retired by then, but with less than a month saved today I cannot call it a promise.
fieldNote: Sara does not treat retirement as automatic; she first wants a **written statement** and real household costs.
Her plan holds room for declining **physical strength** and for continued paid inspection work if needed.

steps.text: Keep safe line shifts and take paid inspection work if able
Put sixty from overtime pay into the emergency envelope
Request a written retirement statement before setting a stopping date
Apply to depot stores if climbing becomes too hard

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could be losing line shifts at 63 with almost no cushion. A real offer of paid training and a named place on another crew would help more than a speech about opportunity. I would also want notice before a roster cut, so Eli and I could decide which bill needs help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I regret starting this trade at 58. I do not. An ordinary repair gives me a little dignity, even while I am learning slower than the younger crew.

headlineQuote: An ordinary repair gives me a little dignity, even while I am learning slower than the younger crew.
portrait: Sara is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who came to the trade through a vocational certificate and still needs supervision.
Her household has **less than one month** of expenses saved, and partner Eli’s bicycle repairs cannot reliably cover rent.
She uses an **AI safety app** daily but checks its output against the printed manual before trusting it.
Across the scenarios, she seeks paid instruction and continued shifts, while treating **retirement** as an unanswered financial question.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could leave Sara without line shifts around age 63 and with almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid training offer**, a named crew placement and advance notice of roster cuts would let the household plan.
